Bird Cladogram Explorer

Type any bird's name — species or genus, Latin or common — and see where it actually sits, computed live from real, current phylogenetic data (McTavish et al. 2025, Open Tree of Life synthesis, 19,302 species). Not limited to Gould's birds: this covers the whole tree.
of ancestry (you can expand further afterwards)
Search matches Latin binomials, common names (eBird/Clements), and genus names.
Each internal node (dot) is one step further back in shared ancestry. Where a branch point has no formal taxonomic name in the dataset — most don't, above genus level — it's labelled here with the genera it actually contains. A wedge means the branch stands in for more than one species collapsed into it — click one to see every species inside it. A dagger (†) marks a species now extinct. A double arrow (⇄) marks a species whose genus is currently disputed between this tree and the eBird/Clements checklist — hover or click it for details.
Sources: McTavish, A. et al. (2025) "A complete and dynamic tree of birds," PNAS 122(18):e2409658122 (Open Tree of Life synthesis, Aves 1.3, CC-BY 4.0) — for the tree itself. Common names and extinction status from the eBird/Clements taxonomy (Cornell Lab of Ornithology), via the auk R package. About 15% of species-level tips in the tree have no common name on file — usually because eBird's own genus placement differs enough from this tree's that automatic matching can't safely bridge the gap, not because the bird is unrecorded.

Glossary

Polytomy
A point where three or more branches meet instead of the usual two. Evolutionary splits are almost always thought of as one lineage dividing into two, so seeing three or more lines meet at a single point looks like an exception to that rule — and in one sense it is. But it doesn't usually mean three species really split from one shared ancestor at exactly the same instant. Most of the time it means the evidence available isn't strong enough to say which pair of lineages split first, so rather than guess at an order it can't support, the tree honestly shows all of them branching from one unresolved point. Less often, it can reflect something real: a genuine burst of very fast, near-simultaneous speciation, where so little time separates the splits that no amount of data could fully untangle the order. Try searching "Goldcrest" and expanding to 5 levels — the Madeira Firecrest and the two subspecies of Common Firecrest all meet at a single point, three lines at once, rather than splitting cleanly two at a time.
Disputed genus placement
Two current, actively-used classifications sometimes disagree about which genus a species belongs in. This tool draws its tree from one authority (Open Tree of Life's synthesis) and its common names from another (eBird/Clements) — when the two disagree about a species' genus, that's not a mistake in either one, it's a live, unresolved question in ornithology. Species aren't dropped into fixed boxes once and for all; as DNA evidence accumulates, working classifications keep shifting, and different expert bodies don't always update in lockstep or reach the same conclusion. Neither authority shown here should be read as "more correct" than the other. Try searching "West Solomons Owl" — this tree places it in Ninox, the hawk-owls; eBird/Clements places it in Athene, the genus of the Little Owl.
